articles.title: Neighborhood air pollution linked to slower brain development in early adolescence
articles.summary: Children living in areas with unhealthy levels of fine particulate matter or ozone showed smaller two-year gains in cognitive performance and brain maturation than demographically matched peers.

articles.title: AI can act exactly like a human, but we still don't think it's conscious
articles.summary: A new study reveals that people draw a surprisingly sharp line between human consciousness and artificial intelligence, even when both behave identically. Researchers found that participants considered even the most responsive AI less conscious than the least responsive human. Yet when asked about "awareness" instead, people judged humans and AI much more similarly.

articles.title: Psilocybin, LSD, and 2C-B leave different fingerprints on the brain, new study suggests
articles.summary: Psilocybin, LSD, and 2C-B all act on the same serotonin receptor, so they are often treated as a single drug class. But brain scans in rats suggest each one shifts the brain’s energy use in its own way, both right away and a week later.

articles.title: Listening to digital jazz might help people manage stress and regulate emotions
articles.summary: Streaming digital jazz might do more than provide background noise. New research shows that algorithm-curated jazz playlists can trigger physical changes in the brain and nervous system, helping listeners manage stress and achieve healthy psychological escapism.

articles.title: Happiness, not awe, may be the better emotional lever for openness to diversity
articles.summary: Researchers expected awe to make people more open to diversity. Instead, in a study of nearly 3,200 adults, a short happy video nudged attitudes in a more inclusive direction, while awe had no measurable effect.

articles.title: The secret to handling stress better may start at breakfast
articles.summary: Your daily routine could have a bigger impact on your ability to handle stress than you realize. A Binghamton University study of approximately 400 college students found that eating breakfast regularly, exercising, sleeping well, and taking fish oil were associated with greater psychological flexibility, which helps people adapt to stressful situations. Poor sleep and unhealthy eating habits, meanwhile, were linked to lower flexibility and resilience.

articles.title: Scientists uncover a hidden map of the brain with 539 distinct regions
articles.summary: Scientists have uncovered a hidden layer of organization in the brain by creating the first detailed 3D map of its lipids, the fatty molecules essential for brain structure and communication. By analyzing millions of measurements from mouse brains, researchers identified 539 distinct chemical zones, revealing patterns and boundaries that traditional brain maps have missed. Surprisingly, even white matter, once thought to be relatively uniform, contains a complex patchwork of chemically distinct regions.

articles.title: High smartphone dependency linked to altered time allocation in teens
articles.summary: Teenagers who overuse smartphones often struggle to manage their own learning later on. A new longitudinal study reveals that digital habits hinder academic skills by displacing study time, rather than by directly increasing academic stress.

articles.title: A drug-free trance can blur the line between self and surroundings
articles.summary: During a deep, self-induced trance, practitioners say their bodies move on their own, their sense of time vanishes, and the boundary between self and world blurs. A small new study found these accounts were accompanied by greater reported inner peace.

articles.summary: Applied behavioral scientists believe their work can influence people’s lives for the better. But what is the most effective way to make that happen? Is it through interventions focused on influencing individual behavior while maintaining freedom of choice? Is it by changing policies and laws, and thereby the systems, that individuals operate within? Is it a combination of the two? articles.title: Scientists may have overlooked a hidden Alzheimer's culprit for decades
articles.summary: For decades, scientists have focused on amyloid beta as a major culprit behind Alzheimer’s disease, spending billions of dollars developing treatments that have often delivered disappointing results. Now, researchers at UC Santa Cruz are drawing attention to a largely overlooked peptide called P3 that could also play a role in the disease. Previously believed to be harmless, P3 can form harmful-looking protein clumps even faster than amyloid beta and may also damage brain cells.
